title: The same names on the funder's board and the recipient's
question: Is anyone listed as an officer, director or trustee of a funder also listed as an officer or director of an organization that funder pays?
finding: 74 funder-and-recipient pairs share at least one rare full name, and the funders in those pairs paid the recipients $39.3 million in 2020 to 2025, $33.9 million of it in years when the name was on both returns. The largest: The Ann & Gordon Getty Foundation for the Arts to San Francisco Symphony ($15.0 million; Gordon P Getty); Kenneth Rainin Foundation to Community Arts Stablization Trust ($4.0 million; Moy Eng; Eric Rodenbeck); Ann & Gordon Getty Foundation to San Francisco Symphony ($2.0 million; Gordon P Getty). In 5 pairs the shared name is a paid officer or employee of the recipient, and in 16 the recipient takes at least half of everything the funder gave to City-paid organizations; no pair shares three or more names.
how: Officers, directors and trustees on the funders' returns (and, for community foundations, the key employees their returns also list) were compared with the officers, directors and key employees on the City-paid organizations' own Form 990s (Part VII), on first and last name with titles and suffixes dropped. 435 names appear in both files; 249 were dropped as too common. A name counts only if it is rare: from how often its first name and its last name occur among the 37,302 distinct names in the funders' returns, the recipients' returns and the City's Form 700 filings, fewer than one other person in 4,000,000 would be expected to share it (the same threshold this project's people screens use). Names whose middle initials disagree are dropped. A pair is shown only if the funder's return also lists a grant paid to that organization, which is the second, independent link. 'While shared' counts grants in years within one year of the name appearing on both returns.
limits: Every row is a name match: same name; not confirmed to be the same person. Where it is the same person, it is usually ordinary: board members of charities often sit on foundations, and family foundations give to the charities their trustees serve. What these records cannot show is whether the person took part in the grant decision; the funder's conflict-of-interest policy and board minutes would.
